newsitem.title: CHINA: China says protects religion, assails critics.
newsitem.headline: China says protects religion, assails critics.

text.p: China on Monday defended its record in protecting religious freedom, saying American critics unfairly distorted its image.

Accusing critics of looking at China "through the wrong end of a telescope", it said the nation was home to more than 100 million followers of various religious faiths and had probably published more Bibles than the United States.
"China grants full rights to freedom of religious belief," said Ye Xiaowen, a senior official of the Bureau of Religious Affairs of the State Council, or cabinet.
"We see the United States big and clearly through our telescope," he told reporters.
"But some people in the United States look through the wrong end of their telescope and they see China small and badly."
Ye made the remarks as conservative American Christian groups gathered forces to block renewal by the U.S. Congress of China's Most Favoured Nation trade (MFN) status.
The powerful Christian Coalition has come out against renewal of MFN, which gives preferential duty treatment to billions of dollars worth of Chinese goods imported into the U.S. market.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has said he would renew the privileges Washington gives to almost all of its trade partners.
House Minority leader Richard Gephardt, who opposes renewal of MFN, said he believed the House of Representatives might vote to overturn the status.

The Chinese official did not mention the debate over MFN though his statements echoed the theme of a lengthy report by the official Xinhua news agency, saying that allegations of religious persecution in China were slanderous and made with ulterior motives.
Religion has made a revival in recent years as Beijing relaxes controls over religious groups, once suppressed as subversive.
But Beijing still keeps a close eye on religious activities and insists that believers practise their faith through officially controlled or sponsored religious organisations.
The State Council's official statement said there were some 10 million Protestants in China, a figure somewhat higher than previous estimates.
Another 20 million Protestants are estimated to practise their faith in secret through underground churches.
The Chinese official said that China had printed 16 million Bibles, and had some 18,000 Christian clergymen and 12,000 churches.
He said there were some four million Catholics.

The U.S.-based Human rights Watch/Asia has said Beijing has stepped up harassment of unauthorised Catholic and Protestant groups in recent years, including tightening controls on contacts with foreigners.
China said it had taken action against a number of cults in recent years but these were quasi-religious groups that had disturbed social order.
"Since the 1980s, a group of cults have formed in some places around China. Some have spread to China from abroad and some have grown and developed on Chinese soil," Xinhua said.
"These quasi-religious organisations, though small in number, have greatly harmed Chinese society," the news agency said.
